$comment: Paired measurements: the SAME quantity on the SAME face, measured by TrueMax
and read off a competitor's own UI. Nothing here is their code, model or
formula — every `theirs` value is a number their product displayed to a
paying user, which is what any customer can read off the screen.
This file exists to answer ONE question: does our pipeline measure the same
thing they do, and if not, is our disagreement systematic. It is deliberately
NOT a calibration set. Fitting anything to their SCORES would be reverse-
engineering their scoring by regression, which is the thing we said we would
not do, merely done statistically instead of by reading code. Their scores are
recorded for context and are never a target.
Add a face by appending to `faces`. Rows only need `ours` and `theirs` in the
SAME units — convert on the way in and say so in `note`. Run:
node tools/benchmark-agreement.mjs
THE ONE RULE THAT IS EASY TO BREAK BY ACCIDENT. Their measured VALUES belong
here; their SCORES must never become a rating anywhere else. This happened
once — their 7.78 for Cavill was rounded to 7.8 and typed into the Calibrate
rating box while their analysis of that same face was open in another tab.
The row looked entirely ordinary and would have made the corpus a regression
onto their formula. It was caught before export, and the Calibrate step now
records where a rating came from and refuses to export a borrowed one.
TWO FINDINGS THE TOOL HAS NOW SURFACED, both needing a measurement fix rather
than a moved ideal:
jawCheekRatio  — reads HIGH by 10.1% on average, but across TWO PEOPLE
(Cavill twice, Bieber once), so it is suggestive and
not established. Rihanna or Gigi settles it either way.
jawFrontalAngle — held out twice for definition mismatch, and both times
ours reads ~26deg high (Bieber 114.1 v 87.9, Cavill 123.1
v 98.0). A mismatch that consistent is a construction we
can identify, not noise.
COUNT PEOPLE, NOT CAPTURES. A `person` field groups repeat captures of one
face. Two photographs of one person share that person's bone structure, so a
construction that disagrees on their face disagrees on both — which reads as
two confirmations and is one. Counting captures let Bieber-plus-Cavill-twice
read as 'all 3 faces' when it was n=2. Set `person` on every new entry; it
defaults to `name` when absent, which is right for a face captured once.
THEIR BANDS ARE PER-PERSON. Constant across two captures of one face, different between
Cavill and Rihanna on all four shared metrics. Sex is the likely axis and their own card
copy argues for it. Gigi Hadid is the control that separates sex from ethnicity: same
sex as Rihanna, different ethnicity. Record the ideal and range on every card from here
on — the bands turned out to carry as much information as the values.
Whatever that comes back as, it stays an observation. TrueMax does not infer ethnicity
from a photograph and does not vary its standards by it.
AN OBSERVATION WE MAY RECORD AND MAY NOT USE. On the two faces that expose Harmony
alongside its own front and side figures, their headline Harmony sits at a fixed point
between them — front weighted 0.614 on Bieber, 0.617 on Rihanna. The two agree to three
decimal places while the ORDERING reverses (Bieber's side beats his front, Rihanna's
front beats her side), which is what makes it a regularity rather than a coincidence of
one face.
Recording it is fair: it is arithmetic on four numbers their UI shows a paying customer.
ADOPTING it is not. Setting our front/side weight to 0.615 because theirs is 0.615 would
be lifting a coefficient out of their scoring formula, which is the whole thing we said
we would not do. Our weighting has to come from our own corpus — from which split
actually predicts our own human ratings — and if that lands near 0.6 it will be because
our faces put it there.

metric                ours    theirs   apart   our score  their score
nasofrontalAngle      134.4   134.7    0.22%   5.2        7.45
totalFacialConvexity  139.9   138.6    0.94%   7.7        9.70

Mean measurement disagreement 1.5 percent. Mean score disagreement 4.6 points out of ten.
A gonial angle one tenth of a degree apart scores 6.8 against 10.0.
Nasolabial is the clearest single case in either product. We measure 114.0 and score it
2.4 out of 10. Their ideal band is 97.0 to 114.0 — our measured value sits INSIDE their
ideal band, at its edge, and we score it in the bottom quarter. Same for ramusMandible:
our 0.690 inverted is inside their 0.62-0.75 band and we give it 2.1.
OUR SIDE LANDMARKS ARE NOT THE PROBLEM. Our side IDEALS are. The 8.23 against our 6.8 is
where our side norms sit, not how badly we place points.
This does not clear the side of everything. #54's repeatability problem is a separate
complaint and still real — a nasolabial that swings 21.9 degrees between two photographs
of one person is unreliable regardless of where its ideal sits. But a well-placed ideal on
a noisy measurement beats a misplaced ideal on the same noisy measurement, and the ideals
are the cheaper half.
WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN NEXT: adopting their bands. Their 97-114 nasolabial band is their
number. Ours has to be re-derived from our own reference set. What this table licenses is
knowing WHICH side ideals to re-derive first, in this order: nasolabialAngle,
ramusMandible, gonialAngle.

cardNote: THEIR IDEAL AND RANGE BANDS ARE IDENTICAL TO THE FIRST CAPTURE, metric for metric:
Bigonial 87.5-91.5 in 68.6-110.4, Jaw Frontal Angle 86.5-92.5 in 54.8-124.2, Jaw Slope

WHAT THIS ESTABLISHES, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. Two captures of one person: the bands do
not move between photographs. That is real and useful — a band is not recomputed per
capture, so a score change between two shots of one face is the MEASUREMENT moving.
This entry previously went further and said a band is a property of the metric rather
than of the person. That was wrong, and could not have been right: two captures of one
man cannot show a band moving between people. See the Rihanna entry — every band she
shares with Cavill sits somewhere else.

cardNote: CORRECTION TO WHAT THIS FILE PREVIOUSLY RECORDED. After the two Cavill captures it said
a band is a property of the METRIC and not of the person, because the bands did not
move between his two photographs. That was true of the observation and wrong as a
generalisation: two captures of one man cannot show a band moving between PEOPLE.
Every band shared with Cavill moves for Rihanna, all four in the same direction:
metric                        Cavill (m)            Rihanna (f)
Face Width to Height          ideal 1.96-2.00       ideal 1.98-2.02
Total Facial Width to Height  ideal 1.34-1.37       ideal 1.32-1.35
Top Third                     ideal 30.0-32.0       ideal 30.4-32.6
Middle Third                  ideal 31.4-33.6       ideal 31.8-33.8
So their bands ARE per-person in some way. Sex is the obvious candidate and their own
card copy supports it: Total Facial Width to Height says 'slightly longer faces benefit
males, while shorter ones suit females', and Rihanna's band for it is indeed the lower
of the two. Face Width to Height says 'higher ratios are preferred for males' — though
there the female band is the HIGHER one, which does not match their own copy.
ONE MAN AND ONE WOMAN CANNOT SEPARATE SEX FROM ANYTHING ELSE ABOUT THEM. Gigi Hadid is
the control: another woman, different ethnicity. Identical bands to Rihanna means the
bands are sex-specific. Different bands means they vary by something else, and their
Lateral Canthal Tilt copy — 'more common and favorable in females and certain ethnic
groups' — says what that something else would probably be.
EITHER RESULT IS AN OBSERVATION, NOT A DESIGN. TrueMax does not infer ethnicity from a
photograph and does not hold different attractiveness standards by ethnicity. Finding
that a competitor does would not change that; it would only tell us why a number of
theirs differs from ours on a given face.
bandComparison: FOURTEEN SHARED METRICS. TWELVE MOVE, TWO DO NOT — and the two that hold still are the
finding, because they rule out the boring explanation that their bands are simply
recomputed per scan.
metric                     ideal (m)      ideal (f)      shift    width m/f
Lateral Canthal Tilt       6.0-7.7        7.8-9.5        +1.8     1.7 / 1.7
Chin to philtrum ratio     2.15-2.45      2.15-2.45      NONE     0.30 / 0.30
Lower Lip to Upper Lip     1.55-1.85      1.55-1.85      NONE     0.30 / 0.30
TEN OF THE TWELVE MOVERS ARE EXACT RIGID TRANSLATIONS — width identical to the decimal,
band moved bodily. The two exceptions are the thirds, off by 0.2 on a one-decimal figure,
which is rounding. Where the range is visible it usually slides by the same amount as the
ideal, so the whole scale translates rather than the target alone.
Midface Ratio is the largest move relative to its own band: +0.12 on a band 0.03 wide,
four band-widths clear. A man and a woman with the SAME midface ratio land in completely
non-overlapping territory on their scale.
THE TWO THAT HOLD STILL MATTER MORE THAN THE TWELVE THAT MOVE. If bands were recomputed
per capture, or drifted with anything incidental, nothing would land byte-identical.
Chin to philtrum is identical in BOTH ideal and range across a man and a woman. So the
bands are fixed tables, selected per person on some axis, and that axis leaves some
metrics alone.
AGAINST THEIR OWN COPY. Of the cards stating a sex effect, the band moves in the stated
direction on seven: eyebrow tilt (female more upturned), jaw slope (higher = more
feminine), canthal tilt, eye separation (higher for females), eye aspect (males narrower),
mouth-to-nose width (females higher with narrower noses), total facial width-to-height
(shorter suits females). Two disagree with their own text:
Face Width to Height   copy says higher suits males; the FEMALE band is higher.
Chin to philtrum       copy says higher favours males and lower suits females; the
band does not move at all.
Lower Lip to Upper Lip makes no sex claim and does not move, which is consistent.
So the axis behaves like sex on most cards and their copy is not a reliable guide to
which. Gigi still decides it: same sex as Rihanna, different ethnicity. The prediction
is now sharp — if the axis is sex, all fourteen of her bands should equal Rihanna's
exactly, including the two that held still.
A SCORING PUZZLE WORTH ONE RE-CHECK. Lower Lip to Upper Lip: Cavill measures 1.33 and
scores 9.0, Rihanna measures 1.32 and scores 9.9 — near-identical values against an
IDENTICAL ideal band of equal width. Either the 9.0 was misread from 9.9, or their score
depends on something beyond the value and the band. Re-read that one card on Cavill.
UNCERTAIN READING, unchanged: Rihanna's Total Facial Width to Height range is recorded
1.05-1.82, but every other range translates rigidly and 1.05-1.62 would preserve Cavill's
width of 0.57 exactly. Probably a misread of 1.62.
